title: Chemise and wrapper styles
subtitle: The outer protective covers of medieval and early modern books
excerpt: A chemise is a secondary covering slipped over a bound book to protect its primary binding. Wrappers and chemises were the principal way that valuable manuscripts and early printed books were protected before modern slipcases. Several distinct styles survive in museum and library collections.
sourceNotes: Cyril Davenport, The Book: Its History and Development (1907): describes wallet, chemise, and limp-vellum wrapper forms in the context of medieval and early modern book production. Douglas Cockerell, Bookbinding and the Care of Books (1901): chapter on historic binding forms including the chemise.

glossaryTerms.definition: A secondary cover slipped over a bound book to protect the primary binding. Often made from leather or thick vellum, with a flap extending past the foredge.
A single piece of dampened vellum (animal skin, not vellum paper) stretched and dried over a text block as a binding covering without boards. Produces a stiff but flexible cover.
A small portable book bound in a long leather chemise with a knotted end that was tucked into a belt or girdle. Carried on the person in the medieval period.

content.text: is a loose outer covering for a bound book. The term also covers a range of secondary covers, protective wrappers, and attached carrying cases. Styles ranged from simple wallet flaps to elaborate cases with closures. Several distinct forms appear across European book history from the tenth to the seventeenth centuries.

The most common form is the wallet chemise: a leather cover with a flap that extends 30 to 50 mm past the foredge and wraps over the front. The flap is sometimes pointed and sometimes rounded. A leather or cord loop glued to the front board holds the flap tip closed. Museum examples in the British Library and the Bodleian Library show wallet chemises in red and white leather from the thirteenth century onward. The same structure is still made by hand bookbinders as a protective outer cover for fine bindings.

is not a chemise but the binding itself. One piece of dampened animal-skin vellum is shaped around the text block and left to dry. This produces a semi-rigid organic covering. It was popular for legal documents and notarial books from the fifteenth to the eighteenth century. Wills, deeds, and parish registers in archives are often limp-vellum bindings. Unlike a board binding, a limp wrapper is reversible: dampen and reshape if it distorts. The chief disadvantage is humidity sensitivity. Vellum responds to every change in atmospheric moisture.

is a small portable book in a long chemise that extended 100 to 150 mm below the lower board. The excess was folded back on itself and knotted, then tucked into the belt or girdle so the book hung spine-down from the waist. The owner would pull the book free, let it drop open from the knot, and read it right-side-up. Examples survive from fifteenth-century Germany and the Low Countries. The book read with the spine at the bottom, which is the opposite of modern convention. Modern hand bookbinders occasionally make reproductions using goat leather.
The drop-spine box as a modern equivalent

The modern equivalent of the chemise is the clamshell or drop-spine box: a rigid case that holds the book in a formed space. Drop-spine boxes are made from bookbinding board and book cloth using almost the same construction as a cased binding. The outer shell lifts away from a fitted inner tray. This form does not require damp leather or specialist animal materials and is the practical approach for making a protective case for a valued hand-bound book at home.

The wallet flap is the form that translates most directly to home bookbinding. It adds no extra materials beyond an extended back board and a strap closure. The limp vellum wrapper requires proper vellum (not vellum paper) and knowledge of how to wet-shape it, which is an advanced topic. The drop-spine box is covered as a separate pattern. The girdle book has no practical modern use but is an interesting reproduction project for historical bookbinding workshops.
